full_judgment:
3. The aforesaid partners, on mutual consent, dissolved the said partnership business on 30th June 1970 and in terms of the deed of dissolution of partnership, the partnership firm namely M/S M Enam Elahi & Brothers was treated on dissolution as the sole proprietary business concern with its goodwill, etc along with moveable, immovable and the liabilities including the case property fell into the share of and was taken over by the former partner Abdul Majid, father of the petitioner. While the petitioner's father Abdul Majid had been in possession and control of the case property as the absolute owner inducted therein tenants and kept a portion in his possession. During the period of liberation war of Bangladesh some members of his family were kidnapped by a group of armed personnel and subsequently they were reportedly killed. The petitioner inherited the property as a sole heir on the death of his father and other members of his family. 

 4. The case property has been commercial building where different commercial proprietorship concerns, partnership firms and limited companies were housed as monthly ejectable tenants since before the independence of Bangladesh. Some of the companies and commercial firms in the case property abandoned their business, left the firms and businesses unattended and one of the such abandoned concerns was a limited company incorporated in the then West Pakistan under the name and style M/S Jaleel Brothers Engineering Ltd, company respondent No. 7 which was declared as an abandoned property and was taken over by the District Management Board having been vested in the Ministry of Commerce. 

 6. The Ministry of Works allowed the said Shamsur Rahman to stay as a tenant under the Ministry as the case property treating the same as an abandoned property under misconception of law. But on representations made by the petitioner the Ministry of Works released it from the list of abandoned property and the Ministry also directed the inmates of the building including the respondent No. 7 M/S Jaleel Brothers to surrender possession to the Superintending Engineer, Abandoned Property, Housing Circle, 88, Motijheel Commercial Area, Dhaka in order to deliver up vacant possession to the petitioner. The government by another memo dated 12-3-82 addressed to six other inmates including the respondent No. 7 Jaleel Brothers to hand over their respective vacant possession to the Superintending Engineer or, in the alternative, to hand over possession to the petitioner directly. Mr Shamsur Rahman as Proprietor of M/S Jaleel Brothers the respondent No. 7 approached the petitioner proposing some unreasonable and illegal terms for becoming a tenant but the petitioner did not accept and demanded the vacant possession in view of the Government direction. 

 9. But suddenly the respondent No. 3 Khondaker Showkat Husain, Deputy Director of Bangladesh Bureau of Anti-Corruption issued a notice dated 26-11-97 (Annexure C) under sections 94/160 of the Code of Criminal Procedure directing the petitioner to appear before Md Ali Akbar Khan and produce the lease deed of the case property. The petitioner appeared, submitted photo copy of the lease deed and the copy of the judgment dated 31-8-97 passed in Writ Petition No. 3223 of 1998. The petitioner in the meantime came to know that a complaint had been lodged by respondent No. 6 as leader of the tenants against whom the suits were filed by the petitioner. The petitioner filed the above mentioned writ petition against the Government and others. 

 10. Petitioner pointed out all about the case property to the respondent Nos. 3 and 4. By Annexure D, dated 4-12-97, the said respondent No. 3 issued another notice asking the petitioner to appear before the respondent No. 4 on 10-12-97 with the documents mentioned therein. 

 13. The respondent No. 2 in their affidavit denied all the material allegations made in the writ petition contending inter alia that the parties of Enam Elahi & Brothers including Abdul Majid left the then East Pakistan before the liberation war was started and, as such, the property has been enlisted as an abandoned property. It has been further stated that the Government permitted Shamsur Rahman to continue as tenant in the case property. The notice dated 26-11-97 and 4-12-97 signed by Deputy Director Khondaker Showkat Husain were served in the interest of proper investigation in the matter because of the fact that complaints have been lodged with the Bureau of Anti-Corruption that the petitioner in collusion with others has been enjoying and possessing abandoned property worth crores of takas claiming ownership and, as such, the petitioner was asked to assist in the matter by appearing before the concerned officer to give his reply and to furnish the necessary documents. 

 21. In support of his above contention Mr Farooqui has referred to a decision in the case of Durga Das vs Emperor, reported in AIR 1943 Lah 28 wherein their Lordships while considering the provisions of sections 94/155 and 165 of the CrPC held as follows: 

 "The combined effect of these provisions of law is that without an order of a competent Magistrate a police officer cannot investigate a non-cognizable case and further that even if he is so authorised, he has to observe the formalities as laid down in sections 94 and 165, Criminal PC, before he can compel the production of any document or seize any incriminating article. In the case of Durga Das reliance was placed in the first instance on ExPC by which the District Magistrate of Lahore authorised Inspector Ram Partap to investigate the case against Gian Chand, Storeman in the office of the Military Engineering Service, Lahore Cantonment. It was, however, later conceded by Mr Ram Partap that the books were not demanded in connection with that case and under this authority he could not investigate a separate non-cognizable case in which he could require the production of Durga Das's books and unless he was so authorised, it is obvious that he could not use any powers which are vested in an officer in charge of a police station or in a police officer making an investigation as contemplated in sections 94 and 165, CPC. This seizure was therefore unauthorised and obviously illegal." 

 23. The argument of Mr SM Munir, is that the Anti-Corruption while investigating an allegation against the petitioner for which a case may be filed against the petitioner in future and for which the Anti-Corruption authority issued the impugned notices within their authority and jurisdiction. In support of his contention he has cited several decisions. We have gone through those decisions and what we find is that the facts of those cited cases and the facts of the instant case are altogether different and distinguishable. We find that the provisions as laid down in the Anti-Corruption Manual are applicable for the offences committed by the public servant and if any private individual commits any forgery the Court of law will initiate proceeding but in the instant case we find no such criminal case of forgery has been filed. So we cannot accept the above argument of Mr Munir. 

 24. Admittedly, the case property had been released by the Government in favour of the petitioner who being the exclusive owner thereof has not obtained the vacant possession of the entire suit property and for which the petitioner had to file a Writ Petition No. 3223 of 1996 against the Government and other persons residing in the case property including the respondent No. 6 and the respondent Nos. 7-14 in the said writ petition the government was directed to hand over the vacant possession to the petitioner. 

 25. It further appears that he filed number of civil suits against the tenants of the case property for their eviction. 

 27. His further argument is that when the respondent Nos. 3 and 4 were aware of the decision of the above mentioned writ petition and pendency of other civil suits, the Anti-Corruption authority ought to have taken their hands off in the matter and refrain from proceeding further, in order to allow the parties to decide the case in the court of law. 

 28. Having regard to the aforesaid aspect of case arising out of the facts and circumstances as discussed above, we are of the view that when a question of right, title and interest relating to any immovable property and where the Court of law was or is in seisin of the court of law the Anti-Corruption Department has no jurisdiction or any authority to hold any inquiry under articles 31 and 50 of Anti-Corruption Manual either suo motu or upon an application filed by any person. The Anti-Corruption may however inquire in a specific case under an order of the Court, otherwise not.
